learning_objectives: Can name and introduce immediate family members (Mutter, Vater, Geschwister, Großeltern) using 'Das ist mein/meine...'
Can ask and answer simple questions about family using 'Hast du...?' and 'Wie heißt dein/deine...?'
Can describe a person's age and origin using 'Er/Sie ist ... Jahre alt' and 'Er/Sie kommt aus...'
prerequisite_knowledge: Basic greetings and farewells: Hallo, Guten Morgen, Tschüss, Auf Wiedersehen
Personal pronouns: ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie, Sie
Verb 'sein' conjugation: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist
Verb 'heißen' conjugation: ich heiße, du heißt, er/sie heißt
Numbers 1–20 for stating age
Basic sentence structure: Subject + Verb + Object (SVO word order)
Introducing oneself: 'Ich heiße... Ich komme aus... Ich wohne in...'

sessions.title: Meine Familie – Familienmitglieder vorstellen

activities.title: Familienfoto-Runde
activities.description: Teacher displays a large illustrated cartoon family portrait on the board (or projector). Students observe the image for 1 minute in silence. Teacher then points to individual family members and says the German term clearly (e.g., 'Das ist die Mutter.'). Students repeat chorally. Then the teacher asks in Vietnamese: 'Ai trong ảnh này trông quen không?' to activate schema. Students briefly discuss in Vietnamese what they see before transitioning to German labels. This culturally familiar lead-in reduces anxiety for Vietnamese learners who value family context.
materials: A3 printed cartoon family portrait (Familienfoto-Poster) with 8 family members labeled
Vocabulary flashcards with German family terms and Vietnamese translation on reverse

activities.title: Familienwortschatz – Einführung mit Grammatik-Notiz
activities.description: Teacher introduces 12 core family vocabulary items using flashcards and the family poster. Each word is presented with: (1) the German noun with article (die Mutter, der Vater, etc.), (2) pronunciation modeled twice, (3) Vietnamese equivalent written on board for reference, (4) a simple example sentence. Teacher explicitly highlights the grammatical gender system as Vietnamese has no articles, explaining: 'In German, every noun has a gender – der (masculine), die (feminine), das (neuter). For family members, you must memorize the article.' Color-coding is used: blue = der, red = die, green = das on the board. Students copy the vocabulary list into their notebooks with a color-coding system. Teacher drills pronunciation of words Vietnamese learners typically struggle with: 'Großmutter' (consonant cluster), 'Geschwister' (sch-sound), 'Schwester' (sw-sound).
materials: Vocabulary flashcards (12 cards, front: German word + article, back: image + Vietnamese translation)
Whiteboard with color markers (blue, red, green)

activities.title: Possessivartikel-Puzzle: mein oder meine?
activities.description: Teacher introduces the possessive articles 'mein' (masculine/neuter) and 'meine' (feminine/plural) with a simple rule card. Since Vietnamese has no grammatical gender, teacher uses a clear analogy: 'Think of mein as a blue label for der-words and das-words, and meine as a red label for die-words and all plurals.' Students receive a gap-fill worksheet with 10 sentences using family vocabulary from the lesson (e.g., 'Das ist ___ Mutter.' / 'Das ist ___ Vater.'). Students complete individually for 3 minutes, then compare in pairs. Teacher reviews answers with whole class, highlighting any patterns. Vietnamese-specific note: teacher draws attention to the fact that Vietnamese uses 'của tôi' for all possessives regardless of gender – this contrast is made explicit.
materials: Grammatik-Regelkarte (mein/meine rule card with color coding)

activities.title: Das ist mein/meine… – Familienvorstellung
activities.description: Students receive a 'Meine Familie' worksheet showing an empty family tree with 6 slots. They write the names of their own family members (or invented names if preferred for privacy). In pairs, Student A holds up their family tree and says 'Das ist mein Vater. Er heißt Minh.' while pointing to each member. Student B listens and asks one follow-up question: 'Wie alt ist er/sie?' Student A answers using 'Er/Sie ist ___ Jahre alt.' Partners then switch roles. Teacher circulates, providing corrective feedback using recasting (repeating the correct form naturally without over-correcting). Vietnamese learner note: Encourage students to use Vietnamese names for family members to make the activity feel authentic and personal.
materials: Vocabulary reference sheet W2-S1-A for support

sessions.title: Über Familie sprechen – Fragen und Antworten

activities.title: Schnelle Wiederholung – Vokabelblitz
activities.description: Teacher holds up family member flashcards rapidly (5 seconds each). Students call out the German word with article chorally. For any errors, the card is placed in a 'practice pile' and revisited at the end. This spaced repetition warm-up takes exactly 5 minutes and reinforces Session 1 vocabulary. Teacher then asks 2–3 individual students: 'Wer ist das?' pointing to the family poster, encouraging full-sentence answers: 'Das ist die Großmutter.'

activities.title: Fragen über die Familie – 'haben' und W-Fragen
activities.description: Teacher introduces the verb 'haben' (to have) conjugation focusing on ich, du, er/sie forms using a clear conjugation table on the board. Key question structures are presented on a grammar poster: (1) 'Hast du Geschwister?' – 'Ja, ich habe eine Schwester / einen Bruder.' / 'Nein, ich habe keine Geschwister.' (2) 'Wie heißt dein/deine...?' – 'Mein/Meine ... heißt...' (3) 'Wie alt ist er/sie?' – 'Er/Sie ist ... Jahre alt.' Teacher explicitly models each Q&A pair twice, then drills with choral repetition. Vietnamese-specific note: The negative 'kein/keine' is highlighted as a key difference from Vietnamese, where negation works differently. Teacher writes: 'Vietnamese: Tôi không có anh chị em = German: Ich habe keine Geschwister' to clarify the structure.
materials: Grammar poster: 'haben' conjugation table + key question structures (Handout W2-S2-A)
Bilingual grammar reference card (German-Vietnamese) for students

activities.title: Dialog-Lückentext – Familie von Lena
activities.description: Students receive a gapped dialogue between two people (Lena and Tom) discussing Lena's family. The dialogue contains 8 gaps for question words, verb forms, and possessive articles. Students complete the dialogue individually (4 minutes), then listen to an audio recording (or teacher reading aloud) to check their answers. Teacher pauses after each gap to confirm the answer with the class. This activity targets reading, listening, and writing simultaneously. The dialogue is set in a realistic context: two university students meeting for the first time, which is culturally relevant for adult learners.
materials: Audio file W2-Dialog-Lena.mp3 OR teacher reads aloud

activities.title: Familieninterview – Informationslücke
activities.description: Students work in pairs with an information-gap activity. Student A has a profile card for 'Familie Müller' with some information missing; Student B has the complementary profile card with different gaps. Students must ask and answer questions to complete their cards using the target structures: 'Hast du...?', 'Wie heißt...?', 'Wie alt ist...?', 'Woher kommt...?' Each student asks at least 5 questions. After 8 minutes, pairs join another pair to form groups of 4. Each student introduces ONE member of their partner's family to the group: 'Das ist Annas Bruder. Er heißt Kevin. Er ist 22 Jahre alt. Er kommt aus München.' Teacher monitors and notes recurring errors for class-level feedback. Vietnamese learner consideration: Pre-teach the honorific consideration – that German families use first names more commonly than Vietnamese families, which is a cultural difference worth noting.
materials: Information-gap profile cards – Set A and Set B (Handout W2-S2-C)

lesson_plans.grammar_focus: Possessive articles in nominative case: mein/meine/mein (my) and dein/deine/dein (your – informal); Conjugation of 'haben' (ich habe, du hast, er/sie/es hat, wir haben); Negation with kein/keine; Nominative case personal pronouns er/sie for referring to third persons
lesson_plans.cultural_note: In German-speaking countries (DACH region – Deutschland, Österreich, Schweiz), family structures have become increasingly diverse. While the traditional 'Kernfamilie' (nuclear family: Mutter, Vater, Kinder) remains common, single-parent families ('Alleinerziehende'), patchwork families ('Patchworkfamilien'), and same-sex parent families are widely accepted and legally recognized. Notably, it is common in Germany for adults to address their parents' friends and even their own grandparents by first name – a contrast with Vietnamese family culture where elaborate honorific titles (ông, bà, chú, cô, etc.) are mandatory. Also worth noting: Germans tend to have smaller families than traditionally seen in Vietnam, with one or two children being most common. The word 'Freund/Freundin' can mean both 'friend' and 'boyfriend/girlfriend' – context determines meaning, a nuance teachers should clarify early to avoid misunderstanding.

homework.description: Students complete a written and speaking homework assignment to reinforce family vocabulary, possessive articles, and the verb 'haben'. The homework is designed to take approximately 30 minutes and includes a creative writing task personalized to the learner's own family.
exercises: Exercise 1 – Mein Stammbaum (My Family Tree): Draw or download a family tree template. Fill in names of at least 6 real or imaginary family members. Label each member with their German family term and article (e.g., 'die Mutter – Lan'). Write one sentence about each member using 'Das ist meine Mutter. Sie heißt Lan. Sie ist 52 Jahre alt.'
Exercise 2 – Lückentext: Complete a 10-item gap-fill exercise on the Zuhause practice sheet (Handout W2-HW-A) focusing on mein/meine/kein/keine in sentences about family.
Exercise 3 – Hörübung (Listening): Listen to audio clip W2-HW-Audio.mp3 (2 minutes, a person describing their family). Answer 5 true/false comprehension questions in German on the answer sheet.

Exercise 4 – Sprachaufnahme (Speaking Practice): Record a 60-second voice memo on your phone introducing your family in German using the sentence frames: 'Ich habe... / Das ist mein/meine... / Er/Sie heißt... / Er/Sie ist ... Jahre alt.' Upload to the class shared folder or bring to next class.

formative: Thumbs up/thumbs down comprehension check after vocabulary presentation – teacher asks 'Mutter – der oder die?' and students respond with gestures
Circulating observation during pair work in Session 1 Activity 4 using a teacher checklist tracking correct use of mein/meine and er/sie pronouns

Mini whiteboard or sticky-note exit ticket at end of Session 2: students write one sentence about a family member using a possessive article – teacher reviews before next class to identify persistent errors
Monitoring of information-gap activity in Session 2 for fluency, accuracy of 'haben' conjugation, and correct question formation
Error log maintained by teacher during speaking activities to inform whole-class feedback at start of next session
assessment.summative: End-of-week oral micro-assessment (5 minutes per student, conducted during Week 3 warm-up): Student presents 4–5 sentences about their own family using the family tree created for homework, then responds to 3 questions from the teacher (e.g., 'Hast du Geschwister?', 'Wie heißt deine Mutter?', 'Wie alt ist dein Vater?'). Assessed on a 3-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of possessive articles and verb forms, (2) Comprehensibility and pronunciation, (3) Ability to respond to spontaneous questions. Written assessment: completed gap-fill homework exercise W2-HW-A is collected and corrected with written feedback.

differentiation.struggling_learners: Provide a bilingual (German-Vietnamese) vocabulary reference card for all activities – students keep this on their desk at all times. Use sentence starters and frame cards during speaking tasks (e.g., 'Das ist mein/meine ___. Er/Sie heißt ___.'). Reduce the information-gap task to 3 questions instead of 5. Allow students to write Vietnamese translations next to German sentences in their notes. Pair struggling learners with a supportive peer during pair work rather than isolating them. For homework, allow the family tree exercise to use only 4 family members instead of 6. Offer a simplified version of the listening homework with slower audio speed. In class, seat struggling learners closer to the board and provide larger-print handouts. Use more visual supports (images, gestures) when presenting new vocabulary. Schedule a 10-minute optional review of Week 1 greetings and introductions for those who need consolidation before proceeding.
differentiation.advanced_learners: Challenge advanced learners to use additional possessive articles: sein/seine (his) and ihr/ihre (her) when describing family members of a third person. Encourage use of additional adjectives: 'Meine Schwester ist groß und lustig.' Introduce the plural forms of family vocabulary as an extension task. In the information-gap activity, ask advanced learners to write a short paragraph (3–4 sentences) summarizing their partner's family after the activity. For homework, add an optional challenge: write a short paragraph (50 words) comparing a German family (from a textbook photo) and their own Vietnamese family, noting one similarity and one difference. Introduce the informal 'du' vs. formal 'Sie' distinction in family contexts as a preview of Week 3 politeness conventions.

review_from_previous: Week 1: Alphabet and pronunciation – revisited through spelling family member names during pair work
Week 1: Personal pronouns ich/du/er/sie – explicitly recycled in mein/meine introduction and family description sentences
Week 1: Verb 'sein' conjugation – reactivated when describing age: 'Er ist 45 Jahre alt'
Week 1: Numbers 1–20 – reviewed functionally when students state ages of family members
Week 1: Self-introduction formula (Ich heiße... Ich komme aus...) – extended to introduce third persons (Er/Sie heißt... Er/Sie kommt aus...)
spaced_repetition.preview_next_week: Week 3 will build directly on this week's family vocabulary by introducing adjective predicates to describe people's appearance and personality (groß, klein, jung, alt, nett, lustig, ruhig). Students will extend from 'Das ist meine Mutter' to 'Meine Mutter ist groß und sehr nett.' The possessive articles introduced this week (mein/meine) will be recycled with new nouns, and the verb 'haben' will reappear in the context of describing physical features: 'Sie hat blaue Augen / schwarze Haare.' This provides a natural communicative bridge: from naming and introducing family members to describing what they look like.

learning_objectives: Can name at least 15 common rooms and furniture items in German (e.g., das Wohnzimmer, der Tisch, das Bett)
Can describe where furniture is located using simple prepositions of place (in, an, auf, unter, neben, zwischen)
Can ask and answer basic questions about their own home using 'Wo wohnst du?' and 'Was gibt es in deiner Wohnung?'
prerequisite_knowledge: Basic German greetings and introductions (Week 1: Hallo, Guten Morgen, Ich heiße...)
Numbers 1–20 for describing floor numbers or room counts (Week 1)
Definite and indefinite articles in nominative case: der, die, das / ein, eine (Week 2)
Basic verb conjugation of 'sein' and 'haben' in present tense (Week 2)
Familiarity with German alphabet and pronunciation rules introduced in Week 1

sessions.title: Meine Wohnung – Rooms and Basic Furniture Vocabulary

activities.title: Bildkarten-Runde: Was siehst du?
activities.description: Teacher displays 8 large illustrated flashcards of rooms (Küche, Wohnzimmer, Schlafzimmer, Badezimmer, Flur, Esszimmer, Arbeitszimmer, Balkon) on the board one at a time. Learners call out any German word they already know for each image. Teacher writes learner suggestions on the board without correcting yet, building on prior knowledge. For Vietnamese learners, teacher notes that Vietnamese homes often have an 'altar room' (phòng thờ) which may not appear in German vocabulary — this brief cultural bridge reduces anxiety and activates schema.
materials: A3-size color flashcards of 8 room types

activities.title: Zimmervokabular einführen – Wortschatz mit Artikeln
activities.description: Teacher introduces 10 target room and furniture words using the TPR (Total Physical Response) method combined with bilingual (German–Vietnamese) vocabulary cards. Each word is presented with: 1) the German word spoken aloud twice, 2) the article highlighted in color (der = blue, die = red, das = green — a color-coding system maintained throughout the course), 3) a picture, and 4) a short Vietnamese gloss on the back of the card for self-study. Teacher drills pronunciation, paying special attention to the German 'ch' in 'Küche' and the umlauts 'ü' and 'ö', which do not exist in Vietnamese phonology. Learners repeat chorally, then in pairs, then individually. Focus words: die Küche, das Wohnzimmer, das Schlafzimmer, das Badezimmer, der Flur, das Bett, der Tisch, der Stuhl, das Sofa, der Schrank.
materials: Bilingual German-Vietnamese vocabulary cards (A5 size, 10 cards per student)
Color-coded article chart (der=blue, die=red, das=green) posted on wall
Teacher's model apartment floor plan poster

activities.title: Zuordnungsübung – Bild und Wort verbinden
activities.description: Learners receive a worksheet showing a simple 5-room apartment floor plan (unlabeled) and a word bank of 10 room/furniture words. Task 1: Label the rooms. Task 2: Match 8 furniture words to the correct room by drawing a line. Teacher circulates and provides immediate corrective feedback. This activity focuses on reading and recognition before production. Vietnamese learners are encouraged to write the article color (B/R/G) next to each word on the worksheet to reinforce grammatical gender.
materials: Worksheet A: Apartment floor plan with word bank (one per student)
Colored pens or pencils (blue, red, green)

activities.title: Partnerübung: Meine Wohnung beschreiben
activities.description: In pairs, Learner A describes their own real or imaginary apartment using the sentence frame: 'Ich habe eine/einen/ein ___. In meiner Wohnung gibt es ___.' Learner B listens and draws a simple sketch of what they hear. Partners then swap roles. Teacher provides a printed sentence scaffold card. This guided speaking task lowers affective filter for Vietnamese learners who may be hesitant to speak freely. After the activity, 2–3 pairs share with the class. Teacher gives gentle error correction on article usage.

activities.title: Exit Ticket: 3 Wörter aufschreiben
activities.description: Each learner writes 3 new vocabulary words they learned today on a sticky note — including the correct article and a self-drawn mini picture. They place the sticky note on a class 'Wortschatzwand' (vocabulary wall) before leaving. Teacher quickly reviews the wall to identify misunderstandings for Session 2 review.

sessions.title: Wo ist das Sofa? – Prepositions of Place and Describing a Room

activities.title: Schnelle Wortschatz-Wiederholung: Memory-Spiel
activities.description: Learners play a quick 5-minute Memory card game in groups of 3. Cards are in pairs: one card shows the German word with article, the other shows the picture. When a learner finds a match, they must say the word aloud correctly (with article) to keep the pair. If the article is wrong, the cards go back. This gamified review reinforces Session 1 vocabulary and article gender simultaneously. Vietnamese learners often find article gender challenging due to the absence of grammatical gender in Vietnamese, so this repeated low-stakes practice is pedagogically essential.
materials: Memory card sets (20 cards per group: 10 word-picture pairs)

activities.title: Präpositionen des Ortes – in, an, auf, unter, neben, zwischen, vor, hinter
activities.description: Teacher uses a large 3D dollhouse model or a projected interactive image of a room to demonstrate prepositions physically. A toy figure (or eraser) is placed in various positions while the teacher narrates: 'Die Katze ist auf dem Tisch. Die Katze ist unter dem Stuhl.' Learners repeat each sentence. Teacher explains dative case briefly and functionally: 'auf dem Tisch' — using a simple 2-column chart (der/das → dem, die → der) without overwhelming grammar detail. A Vietnamese-language grammar note is provided as a printed supplement explaining this is different from Vietnamese which uses no declension. Teacher introduces 5 key preposition sentences using classroom furniture for concreteness.
materials: 3D dollhouse model OR projected room image on screen
Small toy figure or eraser as prop
Printed Vietnamese-language grammar note on dative after location prepositions

activities.title: Hör-Übung: Wo ist was? – Listening and Positioning
activities.description: Learners receive a worksheet showing an empty room outline with furniture labels around it. Teacher reads 8 sentences aloud (at slow, clear A1-appropriate pace), e.g., 'Das Bett steht neben dem Fenster. Der Tisch steht vor dem Sofa.' Learners draw each furniture item in the correct position. Sentences are read twice. After the activity, teacher reveals the answer key via projector and learners self-check. Pronunciation of 'neben,' 'zwischen,' and 'hinter' is drilled again as these sounds are challenging for Vietnamese speakers.
materials: Worksheet B: Empty room diagram with furniture word bank
Audio script (teacher reads aloud) or audio file if available

activities.title: Informationslücken-Aktivität: Zwei Zimmer – welche Unterschiede?
activities.description: In pairs, Learner A receives 'Room A' picture and Learner B receives 'Room B' picture. The rooms are similar but have 6 differences in furniture placement. Without showing their picture, learners describe their room using preposition sentences: 'In meinem Zimmer steht das Sofa neben der Lampe.' They identify the differences by asking: 'Wo ist bei dir das Bett?' This information-gap task requires genuine communicative exchange. Teacher circulates and notes recurring errors on a notepad for group feedback at the end. Pairs who finish early receive an extension card asking them to write 3 sentences describing their own bedroom.
materials: Worksheet C-A: Room picture version A (one set per pair)
Worksheet C-B: Room picture version B (one set per pair)
Sentence scaffold strip: 'In meinem Zimmer ___ das/die/der ___ ___'

activities.title: Kurze Gruppenreflexion + Hausaufgabenerklärung
activities.description: Teacher brings class together for a 6-minute wrap-up. First, teacher gives brief group feedback on 2–3 common errors heard during the information-gap task (without naming individuals), writing correct forms on the board. Learners copy corrections. Then teacher clearly explains the homework assignment using both German and, if needed, Vietnamese for instructions to ensure comprehension. Learners write the homework in their notebooks. Teacher previews next week's topic (sich vorstellen in formellen Situationen) as a motivational bridge.

lesson_plans.grammar_focus: Prepositions of place (Wechselpräpositionen: in, an, auf, unter, neben, zwischen, vor, hinter) used with dative case for static location (Wo? → dative: dem/der/dem). Introduction to 'es gibt + accusative' for stating what exists in a space. Functional use only at A1 level — learners are not expected to produce full declension paradigms but must recognize and use the most common forms: 'auf dem Tisch', 'an der Wand', 'im Schlafzimmer' (contracted in + dem = im).
lesson_plans.cultural_note: In German-speaking countries (Germany, Austria, Switzerland — DACH region), it is common for apartments to be rented without a fitted kitchen ('ohne Einbauküche'), meaning tenants often bring and take their own kitchen furniture and appliances. This is very different from Vietnamese rental norms where furnished apartments are more standard. Additionally, in Germany, it is customary to take off shoes at the entrance ('Flur' or 'Diele'), similar to Vietnamese practice — this cultural parallel can be a positive point of connection for Vietnamese learners. German homes often feature a separate 'Arbeitszimmer' (study/home office), reflecting a cultural value placed on work-life structure. In Switzerland, recycling rules are strict and influence apartment layouts — separate bins for glass, paper, and compost are common even in small flats.

homework.description: Learners complete a written description of their own bedroom or living room (real or imaginary) using at least 8 vocabulary words and 5 preposition sentences learned this week. They also complete a vocabulary learning task using the Anki digital flashcard deck provided by the teacher.
exercises: Exercise 1 (Writing): Write 5–8 sentences describing your bedroom or living room. Use at least 5 different prepositions of place and include the article with each noun. Use the sentence scaffold: 'In meinem Zimmer gibt es ___. Das/Die/Der ___ steht/liegt/hängt ___ dem/der ___.' (Worksheet D provided)

Exercise 2 (Vocabulary): Review all 32 target vocabulary words using the provided Anki flashcard deck (digital, free app). Complete at least 2 review sessions (app tracks completion). Focus on article color-coding.

Exercise 3 (Listening – optional enrichment): Watch a 3-minute YouTube clip of a German person giving a 'Wohnungstour' (apartment tour) — link provided on the course LMS. Write down 5 words you recognize.

formative: Exit ticket at end of Session 1: learners write 3 new vocabulary words with correct article and mini-drawing — teacher reviews before Session 2 to address gaps
Circulating observation during the pair information-gap task in Session 2: teacher uses a simple checklist to note correct/incorrect use of prepositions and article forms for each learner
Self-check after Session 2 listening exercise: learners self-assess against projected answer key and mark errors — teacher collects worksheets to review
Oral monitoring during Memory warm-up game: teacher listens for correct article production and notes patterns
assessment.summative: End-of-week mini-assessment (10 minutes, administered at the start of Week 4 Session 1): 1) Label 10 rooms/furniture images with correct article and noun (10 points). 2) Complete 5 sentences with the correct preposition and dative form based on a room picture (10 points). 3) Write 3 original sentences describing a room shown in a photo (6 points). Total: 26 points. Pass mark: 18/26. Assessment is criterion-referenced against A1 CEFR descriptors for reading and writing. Results used to inform Week 4 remediation grouping.

differentiation.struggling_learners: Provide a pre-filled vocabulary reference card with all 32 target words, articles, and Vietnamese translations during all activities — learners do not need to memorize from scratch but use the card as a scaffold. Reduce the information-gap activity requirement to 3 differences instead of 6. For the homework writing task, reduce the requirement to 4 sentences with a fully completed sentence template. Pair struggling learners with supportive peers (not the strongest) during communicative tasks. Provide the article color-coding system on every worksheet. Offer a short 10-minute optional pre-session review at the start of each session using picture flashcards. Use Vietnamese language explanations for grammar concepts where comprehension is at risk.
differentiation.advanced_learners: Extension card during information-gap task: write a 6-sentence paragraph describing their ideal apartment ('Meine Traumwohnung') using all 8 prepositions. Challenge task: create their own 'Wohnungsanzeige' (apartment listing) similar to those found on Immobilienscout24.de, using authentic online examples as a model. Grammar extension: introduce the Wechselpräpositionen with accusative (movement: Wohin?) as a preview for A2 — brief teacher-led explanation only, no graded assessment. Encourage advanced learners to search for a real German apartment listing online and bring 5 new words to the next session.

review_from_previous: Week 1: Personal pronouns (ich, du, er/sie/es) — recycled in sentence production during speaking tasks ('Ich habe ein Bett. Es steht...')
Week 1: Numbers 1–20 — reactivated when describing apartment size ('Meine Wohnung hat drei Zimmer')
Week 2: Definite and indefinite articles (der, die, das / ein, eine) — directly built upon in this week's article-with-noun vocabulary presentation
Week 2: Verb 'haben' conjugation — recycled in the sentence frame 'Ich habe eine Küche / ein Schlafzimmer'
spaced_repetition.preview_next_week: Week 4 will focus on 'Alltag & Tagesablauf' (Daily Routines). The apartment vocabulary from Week 3 provides the spatial context for daily routine verbs: learners will describe what they do in each room (in der Küche frühstücke ich, im Schlafzimmer schlafe ich). The prepositions of place will be extended to prepositions of direction (Wechselpräpositionen with accusative: Ich gehe in die Küche). The 'es gibt' structure will also recur when describing daily activities.

learning_objectives: Can order food and drinks in a simple restaurant or café using basic phrases such as 'Ich möchte...', 'Ich nehme...' and 'Bitte'
Can understand simple menu items and prices when spoken slowly and clearly or presented in writing
Can ask for the bill and respond to basic questions from a waiter such as 'Was möchten Sie?' and 'Zusammen oder getrennt?'
prerequisite_knowledge: Numbers 1–100 (for understanding prices)
Basic greetings and polite expressions: 'Guten Tag', 'Bitte', 'Danke', 'Auf Wiedersehen'
Subject pronouns: ich, Sie (formal), wir
Present tense of 'sein' and 'haben'
Indefinite articles: ein, eine (Nominativ)
Basic question formation: Was? Wie viel?

sessions.title: Im Café – Speisekarte und erste Bestellungen

activities.title: Bilder raten – Was ist das?
activities.description: Teacher displays 10 flashcard images of common German café/restaurant items (Kaffee, Tee, Wasser, Bier, Cola, Kuchen, Brot, Suppe, Salat, Schnitzel) on the projector one by one. Learners call out any word they already know in German, Vietnamese, or English. Teacher provides the German word and learners repeat chorally. This activates prior knowledge and creates a low-anxiety entry point. Vietnamese learners benefit from visual anchoring before new vocabulary input.
materials: Flashcard image set (10 food & drink items, printed or digital)

activities.title: Die Speisekarte – Vokabeln einführen
activities.description: Teacher distributes a simple one-page mock German café menu ('Café Mitte – Speisekarte') with 8 food items and 6 drink items, each with a photo, the German word, its article (der/die/das), plural form, and price in euros. Teacher reads each item aloud using natural speed then slightly slower pace. Learners listen and point to items. Then learners repeat each item in a 'Listen–Repeat–Point' cycle. The menu also includes Vietnamese translations in a lighter font as a scaffold, which can be folded away for production tasks. Teacher highlights article color-coding: der = blue, die = red, das = green — a visual strategy proven effective for Vietnamese learners who have no grammatical gender in L1.
materials: Printed mock Speisekarte 'Café Mitte' (A4, color-coded by gender)
Audio recording or teacher voice model

activities.title: Was kostet das? – Preise üben
activities.description: Learners work in pairs. Partner A holds the menu and reads out an item ('Der Kaffee kostet einen Euro fünfzig'). Partner B writes the price they hear on a mini-answer sheet. After 5 items, partners swap roles. Teacher monitors and provides corrective feedback focusing on number pronunciation (common difficulty: 13 vs. 30, 15 vs. 50 for Vietnamese learners). Full class check at end with teacher writing prices on board.
materials: Mini answer sheet with item names and blank price fields

activities.title: Redemittel einführen – Bestellen im Café
activities.description: Teacher presents a structured dialogue card showing the essential speech acts for ordering. The card shows two columns: KELLNER (waiter) and GAST (guest). Waiter lines: 'Was möchten Sie?', 'Bitte sehr!', 'Zusammen oder getrennt?'. Guest lines: 'Ich möchte [item], bitte.', 'Ich nehme [item].', 'Die Rechnung, bitte.' Teacher models each phrase with natural gesture and intonation. Learners repeat. Teacher then plays a short audio dialogue (90 seconds) set in a German café. Learners listen and check which phrases from their card they hear. Teacher explicitly contrasts 'ich möchte' (polite modal, preferred in restaurants) with 'ich will' (blunt, impolite in service contexts) — a nuance that Vietnamese learners frequently miss.
materials: Dialogue card (Redemittel Bestellen – laminated or printed)
Audio file: 'Im Café – Dialog 1' (MP3 or teacher-performed)

sessions.title: Rollenspiel & Kommunikation – Wir bestellen!

activities.title: Blitzrunde – Vokabeln auffrischen
activities.description: Quick 5-minute review of Session 1 vocabulary using a 'Zap' card game. Each learner holds 3–4 vocabulary cards face down. Teacher points to a learner who must flip a card and say the German word with its article. If correct, they keep the card. If incorrect, the card goes to the 'Zap' pile. The learner with the most cards after the round wins. This kinesthetic review technique keeps Vietnamese adult learners engaged and reinforces article-noun pairing through repetition.
materials: Vocabulary card set (32 cards: German word + image on front, article color-coded)

activities.title: Dialog üben – Schritt für Schritt
activities.description: Learners receive a gapped dialogue transcript. Teacher reads the full dialogue aloud while learners follow. Learners then fill in the gaps (Kellner or Gast lines) using their Redemittel card as support. Pairs read the completed dialogue together. Teacher circulates and provides immediate oral feedback. Common pronunciation focus for Vietnamese learners: the German 'ö' in 'möchte' and the final consonant cluster in 'bitte' — teacher drills these specifically using minimal pair repetition.
materials: Gapped dialogue worksheet (3 variants of different difficulty)

activities.title: Rollenspiel – Im Restaurant
activities.description: Learners perform a structured role-play in groups of 3: one Kellner and two Gäste. Each group receives a different role card set. Gast cards specify what they want to order (with picture prompts). Kellner cards provide the full service script. Groups rehearse for 3 minutes, then perform in front of another group (not the whole class — reduces Vietnamese adult learner anxiety about public performance). Observer group fills in a simple peer-feedback form: Did the Gast use 'Ich möchte'? Did they say 'Bitte'? Did they ask for the bill? Teacher rotates and records notes for formative assessment. After practice, 2 volunteer groups perform for the whole class.
materials: Role card sets (Kellner + Gast A + Gast B) — 4 different versions

activities.title: Akkusativ mit 'möchte' – kurze Grammatikerklärung
activities.description: Teacher draws a simple 2-column table on the board showing Nominativ vs. Akkusativ for ein/eine. Focus is ONLY on the masculine change (ein → einen) as this is the only visible change at A1 level. Example: 'Das ist ein Kaffee' (Nom.) vs. 'Ich möchte einen Kaffee' (Akk.). Teacher uses Vietnamese metalinguistic note: similar to how Vietnamese uses different counting words (classifiers) for different nouns, German changes the article. This cross-linguistic bridging strategy improves retention for Vietnamese learners. Learners complete 6 quick written sentences transforming nominative to accusative. Immediate whole-class correction.

activities.title: Exit Ticket – Drei Sätze schreiben
activities.description: Each learner writes 3 sentences on a sticky note before leaving: (1) Something they would order: 'Ich möchte...', (2) A price they remember: '[Item] kostet...', (3) One new word they learned today. Teacher collects sticky notes to gauge comprehension and adjust next session if needed. This low-stakes writing task also activates metacognitive awareness — important for self-directed adult learners.

lesson_plans.grammar_focus: Modal verb 'möchte' (polite form of mögen) in present tense for ordering; introduction to Akkusativ with indefinite articles: ein → einen (masculine), eine (feminine, no change), ein (neuter, no change); sentence structure: Subject + möchte + Akkusativ-Objekt + bitte
lesson_plans.cultural_note: In German-speaking countries (DACH region), it is standard and expected to greet the waiter when they approach ('Guten Tag!') and to say 'Danke' when receiving food or the bill. Tipping (Trinkgeld) is customary but not obligatory — rounding up the bill or adding 10% is common. Unlike in Vietnam where the bill is often brought automatically, in Germany/Austria/Switzerland you must explicitly ask: 'Die Rechnung, bitte.' Splitting the bill ('getrennt zahlen') is very common and not considered impolite. Tap water ('Leitungswasser') is not typically served for free in restaurants — learners should ask for 'Mineralwasser' (sparkling) or 'stilles Wasser' (still). In Austria, ordering a 'Melange' (coffee with milk) is more common than 'Cappuccino'. In Switzerland, 'Grüezi' replaces 'Guten Tag' in the German-speaking cantons.

homework.description: Learners consolidate vocabulary and practice the ordering dialogue independently using a combination of digital and paper exercises.
exercises: Complete the online vocabulary quiz on the class platform (Quizlet set 'Woche 4 – Essen & Trinken'): match German food/drink words with images — 20 items, target 85% accuracy
Write a short ordering dialogue (8–10 lines) between a Kellner and a Gast ordering 2 food items and 2 drinks, paying separately — use the Redemittel card as reference

Listen to audio track 'Im Restaurant – Dialog 2' (provided as MP3 link) and answer 5 comprehension questions on the worksheet: What does the guest order? How much does it cost? Do they pay together or separately?
Optional extension: Find a real German café menu online (e.g., from a Vienna or Berlin café website) and write down 5 items you would order with prices — prepare to share next lesson

formative: Observation during pair and group role-plays: teacher uses a clipboard checklist to note whether each learner uses 'ich möchte', correct articles, and polite phrases
Exit ticket sticky notes collected at end of Session 2: teacher reviews to identify misconceptions about articles or vocabulary gaps before next lesson
Peer feedback forms from role-play activity: learners assess each other against 3 observable criteria (polite form used, correct item named, bill requested)
Circulating during the gapped dialogue task: teacher notes which learners need additional support with Akkusativ article change
assessment.summative: End-of-week role-play performance test (conducted in Week 4 final session or start of Week 5): Each learner performs a 2-minute role-play as a Gast in a café scenario drawn randomly from 4 scenario cards. Assessed using a 3-criterion rubric: (1) Communicative Achievement — did the learner successfully order and ask for the bill? (2) Vocabulary — did they use at least 5 target words correctly? (3) Accuracy — did they use 'ich möchte' with the correct Akkusativ article at least twice? Scoring: 0–2 per criterion, maximum 6 points. Pass = 4/6.

differentiation.struggling_learners: Provide a fully completed Redemittel card with sentence frames to fill in (e.g., 'Ich möchte _____, bitte.') rather than requiring free production. Allow learners to keep the Vietnamese translation column visible on the menu during role-plays. Reduce role-play vocabulary scope to 4 drinks and 4 food items instead of the full menu. Pair struggling learners with a supportive peer as Gast (not Kellner) in the first role-play so they have a model to follow. Offer a pre-recorded model dialogue they can listen to at home multiple times. Use additional gesture-based drills for 'möchte' pronunciation. Provide a labeled article chart (der/die/das with color) to keep on the desk throughout all activities.
differentiation.advanced_learners: Challenge learners to perform the role-play without any support cards, improvising responses to unexpected questions. Introduce additional phrases: 'Haben Sie auch vegetarische Gerichte?', 'Ich bin allergisch gegen...', 'Das schmeckt sehr gut!' Encourage learners to write a short restaurant review (3–4 sentences) using adjectives learned in previous weeks. Ask them to research and present one interesting food fact about a DACH country to the class next session (2-minute mini-presentation). Introduce informal register: 'was nimmst du?' vs formal 'was nehmen Sie?' and discuss when each is appropriate.

review_from_previous: Week 1: Greetings and farewells — reactivated in role-play openings ('Guten Tag!' / 'Auf Wiedersehen!')
Week 2: Numbers 1–100 — recycled through price recognition and listening activities ('Das kostet drei Euro zwanzig')
Week 3: Verb conjugation in present tense (ich/Sie forms) — reinforced through 'ich möchte', 'ich nehme', 'ich zahle'
Week 3: Indefinite articles ein/eine — extended into Akkusativ transformation this week
spaced_repetition.preview_next_week: Week 5 will focus on 'Einkaufen im Supermarkt' (shopping for groceries). The food and drink vocabulary acquired this week will be directly recycled in supermarket contexts. Learners will extend Akkusativ knowledge to include definite articles (den/die/das) and be introduced to quantities and containers ('eine Flasche Wasser', 'ein Kilo Äpfel'). The polite modal 'ich möchte' will continue to feature in shop assistant interactions, providing a direct structural bridge from restaurant to retail settings.

learning_objectives: Can tell and ask for the time using both official (24-hour) and colloquial (12-hour) clock formats in German
Can describe a simple daily routine using common time expressions and separable verbs (aufstehen, aufwachen, einschlafen)
Can ask and answer simple questions about daily schedules using 'Wann...?', 'Um wie viel Uhr...?', and 'Was machst du um...?'
prerequisite_knowledge: Numbers 1–60 (covered in Week 2)
Basic subject pronouns: ich, du, er, sie, wir (covered in Week 1)
Present tense conjugation of regular verbs: machen, arbeiten, lernen (covered in Week 3)
Basic vocabulary for activities: essen, trinken, schlafen, gehen (covered in Week 3–4)
Days of the week: Montag bis Sonntag (covered in Week 4)

sessions.title: Wie spät ist es? – Telling the Time

activities.title: Zahlen-Blitz: Number Lightning Round
activities.description: Teacher displays numbers 1–60 on flashcards or PowerPoint slides rapidly. Learners call out the number in German as a class. Then teacher points to a digital clock image showing a full hour (e.g., 08:00) and asks 'Was ist das?' to activate prior number knowledge and bridge to telling time. This recycles Week 2 vocabulary and lowers affective filter by starting with known content. Vietnamese learners often feel confident with numbers, so this builds positive momentum.
materials: PowerPoint slide with digital clock images showing full hours

activities.title: Die Uhr – Analogue Clock Presentation
activities.description: Teacher introduces a large analogue clock visual (printed or projected). Step 1: Teach full hours – 'Es ist ein Uhr / zwei Uhr … zwölf Uhr.' Drill chorally. Step 2: Introduce half hours – 'Es ist halb zwei' (= 1:30). Highlight the Vietnamese-German contrast: in Vietnamese, 1:30 is described as 'past 1' concept, whereas German 'halb zwei' means 'half to two' – teacher explicitly addresses this cognitive challenge. Step 3: Introduce quarter hours – 'Viertel nach drei' (3:15) and 'Viertel vor vier' (3:45). Write key structures on the board in a clear colour-coded table. Step 4: Briefly introduce the 24-hour official format used in Germany for transport, TV schedules, and formal contexts: 'Der Zug fährt um 15:30 Uhr.' Use a Deutsche Bahn timetable image as cultural anchor.
materials: Large printable analogue clock (A3 poster or projected image)
Deutsche Bahn timetable screenshot (printed or projected)

activities.title: Ticktack – Clock Drill Pairs
activities.description: Learners work in pairs. Each pair receives a set of 10 clock face cards (Lernkarten) showing different times (full hours, half hours, quarter past, quarter to). Partner A holds up a card; Partner B says the time in German. Then roles switch. Teacher monitors and provides immediate corrective feedback using recasting (repeating the correct form naturally). A scoreboard on the board tracks which pair gets the most correct in 5 minutes to add mild competitive motivation, which aligns well with Vietnamese classroom culture preferences.
materials: Set of 10 clock face cards per pair (printed and laminated or cut from handout)

activities.title: Wie spät ist es? – Mingling Activity
activities.description: Each learner receives a card with one clock time written on it (they do not show it to others). Learners stand up and mingle. They ask a partner 'Wie spät ist es?' and their partner answers based on their own card, then asks back. Learners note down 5 different times they hear on a simple recording sheet. After the activity, teacher elicits answers and writes them on the board. This provides meaningful repetition in a communicative context and gives learners practice initiating and responding to questions.
materials: Time cards (one per learner, 15–20 different times pre-prepared)

activities.title: Exit Ticket: Drei Uhrzeiten
activities.description: Teacher displays three clock faces on the projector. Each learner writes the time in German on a small slip of paper and hands it in as they leave. Teacher uses this as formative data to identify which time formats (especially 'halb' and 'Viertel vor') need reinforcement at the start of Session 2. Slips take less than 2 minutes and give immediate diagnostic information.
materials: Small paper slips (index cards or cut paper)

sessions.title: Mein Tagesablauf – Describing Daily Routines

activities.title: Uhrzeit-Feedback & Schnellwiederholung
activities.description: Teacher returns exit tickets from Session 1, briefly reviews the three most common errors (typically 'halb' constructions and 'Viertel vor'). Quick 3-minute flashcard review of clock times using digital dice or random clock generator projected on screen. Learners answer chorally and then individually when called. This spaced review within the same week solidifies retention before introducing new content.
materials: Online random clock generator or PPT with clock faces

activities.title: Tagesablauf-Vokabeln & Trennbare Verben
activities.description: Teacher presents a visual daily routine timeline for a fictional character 'Anna' using a poster or PPT with 8 illustrated scenes across a day. For each scene, teacher introduces the key verb and sentence: 'Um 6 Uhr wacht Anna auf. Um 6:30 Uhr steht sie auf. Um 7 Uhr frühstückt sie...' Key focus: introduce separable verbs aufwachen, aufstehen, anziehen, einschlafen. Draw explicit attention to verb-second rule and that the prefix goes to the end: 'Ich stehe um 6 Uhr AUF.' Use colour coding (prefix in red, stem in blue) on the board. Provide a Vietnamese translation gloss in the vocabulary handout for Week 5 since direct translation is an effective scaffold at A1 for Vietnamese adult learners. Also introduce time adverbials: morgens, mittags, abends, nachts, dann, danach, zuerst.
materials: Anna's Tagesablauf poster / PPT (8 illustrated scenes)
Vocabulary handout with German word, Vietnamese gloss, and example sentence
Colour-coded verb table on whiteboard (separable verbs)
Blu-Tack or magnets for poster display

activities.title: Annas Tag – Sentence Building Strips
activities.description: Learners work in groups of 3. Each group receives an envelope with sentence strips of Anna's daily routine cut into pieces (subject, separable verb stem, time phrase, prefix on separate cards). Groups must reconstruct 8 grammatically correct sentences about Anna's day and arrange them in chronological order on their desk. This tactile activity suits diverse learning styles and encourages discussion in the group. Teacher circulates and prompts with questions like 'Wo ist das Präfix?' to draw attention to separable verb structure.
materials: Sentence strip envelopes (one per group of 3)
Pre-cut sentence component cards (verb stems, prefixes, time phrases, subjects)
Answer key poster revealed at end

activities.title: Mein Tagesablauf – Interview & Notizen
activities.description: Learners interview a partner about their real daily routine using a structured question frame provided on the handout: 'Um wie viel Uhr stehst du auf? / Um wie viel Uhr frühstückst du? / Wann gehst du zur Arbeit/zur Schule? / Wann schläfst du ein?' Partner B answers truthfully; Partner A notes the times in a table. Then roles switch. Afterwards, 2–3 learners share interesting findings with the class: 'Linh steht um 5:30 Uhr auf!' This generates authentic communicative interaction and personalises learning, which increases retention. Note: Vietnamese adult learners often work early shifts or have family obligations – teacher should affirm diverse routines to build inclusive classroom culture.
materials: Structured interview handout with question prompts and a table for recording answers
Vocabulary support card (Tagesablauf verbs + time expressions)

activities.title: Mein Tag in 3 Sätzen – Written Summary
activities.description: Learners write 3 sentences about their own daily routine using the new separable verbs and time expressions. Teacher collects these as a formative writing sample. Before collecting, ask 2–3 volunteers to read their sentences aloud – this provides a brief oral production check and ends the session with a sense of accomplishment. Teacher previews homework briefly.
materials: Lined paper or back of interview handout

vocabulary_target: zur Arbeit gehen (to go to work)
Mittagspause machen (to take a lunch break)
Wie spät ist es? (What time is it?)
Um wie viel Uhr...? (At what time...?)
lesson_plans.grammar_focus: Separable verbs (Trennbare Verben) in the present tense: aufstehen, aufwachen, anziehen, einschlafen – with focus on prefix separation to sentence-final position (e.g., 'Ich stehe um 6 Uhr auf.') and the time prepositional phrase 'um + accusative time expression' for clock times
lesson_plans.cultural_note: In German-speaking countries (Germany, Austria, Switzerland), punctuality (Pünktlichkeit) is a deeply valued cultural norm. Being on time for appointments, work, and social meetings is considered respectful. The 24-hour clock is widely used in official contexts: train schedules (Deutsche Bahn), TV programming, and formal invitations will state times like '15:45 Uhr' rather than 'Viertel vor vier'. However, in casual conversation among friends, Germans use the 12-hour colloquial system. Swiss German speakers may use slightly different informal time expressions. Additionally, the traditional German Mittagspause (lunch break) was historically 1–2 hours long and some shops still close midday in smaller towns and in Austria, which may surprise Vietnamese learners accustomed to different business hour norms.

homework.description: Learners complete three exercises to consolidate clock reading, separable verb usage, and routine description, preparing them for a short speaking check at the start of the following week.
exercises: Exercise 1 – Wie spät ist es? (Reading): Look at 8 clock face images in the handout and write the time in German in both colloquial format (e.g., Viertel nach drei) and official format (e.g., 15:15 Uhr)

Exercise 2 – Mein Tagesablauf (Writing): Write 6–8 sentences describing your own daily routine using at least 4 different separable verbs and 4 different time expressions from the vocabulary list. Underline all separable verb prefixes.

Exercise 3 – Lückentext (Gap-fill): Complete a short paragraph about Thomas's daily routine by filling in the correct form of the separable verb provided in brackets (aufstehen, frühstücken, anziehen, einschlafen) and the missing prefix in the correct position.
Bonus (optional): Record a 60-second voice memo on your phone describing your morning routine in German and listen back to check for verb-second word order and prefix placement.

formative: Session 1 Exit Ticket: Learners write 3 clock times from projected images – teacher reviews before Session 2 to identify gaps in 'halb' and 'Viertel vor' understanding
Observation during Clock Drill Pairs: teacher circulates and notes learners struggling with time formats, particularly the counterintuitive 'halb' construction for Vietnamese speakers
3-sentence written summary at end of Session 2: teacher scans for correct separable verb prefix placement and appropriate time expressions before returning with brief written feedback next session
Interview activity monitoring: teacher notes learners who avoid separable verbs or revert to infinitive forms, flagging need for additional structural support
assessment.summative: End-of-week mini-task (administered at start of Week 6, first 10 minutes): Each learner receives a simple 'Was macht Lena?' information card describing a character's daily schedule with times given only in numbers (e.g., 07:30, 12:00, 22:00). The learner must write 5 complete sentences describing Lena's routine using separable verbs in the correct present tense form, the correct German time expression (colloquial format), and at least 2 different time adverbials (zuerst, dann, danach, morgens, abends). Assessed using a simple 3-point rubric: vocabulary use, verb structure accuracy, and comprehensibility.

differentiation.struggling_learners: Provide a laminated reference card with the clock face diagram showing all key time expressions labelled (Es ist ein Uhr / halb zwei / Viertel nach drei / Viertel vor vier) that learners can keep on their desk during activities. For separable verbs, provide a colour-coded sentence template: [Ich] [STEM] [time phrase] [PREFIX]. Allow learners to use Vietnamese glosses in their written homework. During pair work, strategically partner struggling learners with supportive mid-level peers. Reduce the gap-fill homework to 4 items instead of 8. During the interview activity, provide a fully pre-written model dialogue that learners can adapt rather than generating from scratch.
differentiation.advanced_learners: Challenge advanced learners to describe their daily routine using both the 12-hour colloquial format AND the 24-hour official format in the same text. Introduce the modal verb 'müssen' informally: 'Ich muss um 6 Uhr aufstehen' as a preview of A2 content. Ask them to write a short comparison between a typical Vietnamese daily schedule and a typical German daily schedule based on the cultural note, using connectors 'aber' and 'und'. During the mingling activity, challenge them to ask two additional questions beyond the prompt card. Bonus homework: research the concept of 'Kaffeepause' in German offices and write 2–3 sentences explaining it in German.

review_from_previous: Numbers 1–60 (Week 2): recycled in clock-reading activities throughout both sessions
Present tense conjugation of regular verbs (Week 3): foundation for separable verb conjugation patterns introduced this week
Days of the week (Week 4): briefly reactivated during the interview activity when learners may ask 'Was machst du am Montag morgens?' as a natural extension
Basic activity vocabulary: essen, trinken, schlafen, gehen (Weeks 3–4): integrated into daily routine sentences and serve as known anchors for new separable verb forms
spaced_repetition.preview_next_week: The daily routine vocabulary and time expressions introduced this week directly scaffold Week 6 topic 'Familie & Wohnen' – learners will describe family members' routines and talk about who does what at home and at what time, building on separable verbs with third-person singular conjugation (er/sie steht auf, schläft ein) and introducing possessive articles (mein, meine) in context.

learning_objectives: Can name at least 12 body parts in German and point to them correctly when prompted
Can express basic health complaints using 'Ich habe Schmerzen / Ich habe Kopfschmerzen / Mir ist schlecht' in simple sentences
Can understand and respond to simple questions about health such as 'Was fehlt Ihnen?' and 'Wie geht es Ihnen?' in a pharmacy or doctor's office context
prerequisite_knowledge: Basic verb conjugation in present tense (haben, sein) from Weeks 1–3
Numbers 1–100 for describing age and symptoms (Week 4)
Basic question words: Was, Wie, Wo (Week 2)
Indefinite and definite articles (der, die, das, ein, eine) from Weeks 3–4
Simple yes/no question formation from Week 5
Basic greetings and introductions from Week 1

sessions.title: Körperteile – Den menschlichen Körper kennenlernen

activities.title: Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes – Deutsch Version
activities.description: Teacher leads the class in the German version of 'Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes' (Kopf, Schultern, Knie und Zehen). Play the song once in English first for familiarity, then switch to German. Learners stand up, listen, and physically touch each body part as it is mentioned. Repeat 3 times at increasing speed. This kinesthetic warm-up activates prior knowledge of body vocabulary and uses Total Physical Response (TPR) which is highly effective for Vietnamese adult learners who respond well to action-based repetition. Teacher writes each body part on the whiteboard as it appears in the song.
materials: Audio track: 'Kopf, Schultern, Knie und Zehen' (YouTube or MP3)

activities.title: Der Körper – Körperteile benennen
activities.description: Teacher displays a large, labelled diagram of the human body (front and back) on the projector or as a printed A3 handout. Introduce 14 core body parts with their articles: der Kopf, das Gesicht, das Auge (die Augen), die Nase, der Mund, das Ohr (die Ohren), der Hals, die Schulter (die Schultern), der Arm (die Arme), die Hand (die Hände), der Bauch, das Bein (die Beine), das Knie (die Knie), der Fuß (die Füße). Teacher models pronunciation clearly twice for each word; Vietnamese learners should pay special attention to the German 'ü' in Füße and 'ä' in Hände as these vowel sounds do not exist in Vietnamese. Use color-coding on the board: blue for masculine (der), red for feminine (die), green for neuter (das). Learners repeat chorally and then individually. Drill pronunciation of difficult sounds. Provide a bilingual Vietnamese–German vocabulary card for take-home reference.
materials: A3 body diagram handout (labelled in German)

activities.title: Zeig mir! – TPR Körperteil-Spiel
activities.description: Teacher calls out a body part in German (e.g. 'Die Nase!'). Learners must point to the correct body part on their own body as fast as possible. After 2 rounds with teacher leading, learners take turns being the 'caller' in small groups of 4. This reinforces the vocabulary in a low-anxiety, physical way. In the second phase, teacher holds up picture flashcards of isolated body parts and learners call out the correct German word with the article. Wrong article usage is gently corrected by the group echoing the correct form.
materials: Flashcards with isolated body part images (printed or digital)

activities.title: Beschrifte den Körper – Lückendiagramm
activities.description: Learners receive a blank body diagram (unlabelled silhouette) and a word bank containing 14 body part words without articles. Task 1: Write the correct word next to each body part. Task 2 (extension): Add the correct article (der/die/das) using the color-coding system from the presentation. Learners work individually for 5 minutes, then compare answers in pairs. Teacher circulates and provides feedback. Review answers as a whole class using the projector. Special attention to common Vietnamese learner errors: confusing 'der Arm' vs 'das Bein' due to article assignment not following logical patterns, and plural forms.

activities.title: Exit Ticket – Wie heißt das auf Deutsch?
activities.description: Teacher points to 5 body parts on a poster silently. Each learner writes the German word with article on a sticky note or small slip of paper and hands it to the teacher as they leave. This quick formative check takes 2 minutes and gives the teacher instant data on which body parts need review at the start of Session 2. Teacher reviews slips before Session 2 begins.
materials: Sticky notes or small paper slips

sessions.title: Gesundheit & Beschwerden – Beim Arzt und in der Apotheke

activities.title: Körperteil-Bingo – Wiederholung
activities.description: Each learner receives a 3x3 bingo card with 9 body part images (randomly arranged, different for each card). Teacher calls out German body part names. Learners cross off the matching image. First learner to cross off all 9 calls 'Bingo!' and reads back all 9 words aloud with articles to confirm. Play 2 rounds. This revises Session 1 vocabulary in a motivating format. Vietnamese adult learners respond particularly well to game-based revision as it reduces anxiety around recall.
materials: Printed bingo cards (one per learner, 6 different variants)

activities.title: Ich bin krank! – Beschwerden und Schmerzen
activities.description: Teacher introduces health complaint vocabulary and key phrases using a short illustrated story on slides: 'Anna hat Kopfschmerzen. Sie geht zum Arzt.' Present the following: Schmerzen haben (to be in pain), Kopfschmerzen (headache), Bauchschmerzen (stomachache), Halsschmerzen (sore throat), Rückenschmerzen (back pain), Fieber haben (to have a fever), Husten (cough), Schnupfen (runny nose), müde sein (to be tired), krank sein (to be sick). Introduce two key structures: 'Ich habe + [body part] + -schmerzen' and 'Ich habe + Fieber/Husten/Schnupfen'. Explain the compound noun structure (Körperteil + Schmerzen) – this concept is familiar to Vietnamese learners as Vietnamese also uses compound words extensively (đau đầu = head-pain). This cross-linguistic connection should be made explicit. Model pronunciation with emphasis on the -sch- cluster which is challenging for Vietnamese speakers. Display a visual pain scale 1–10 and teach 'Die Schmerzen sind stark / schwach / mittel'.
materials: PowerPoint/Google Slides with illustrated health scenarios

activities.title: Was fehlt ihnen? – Symptom-Zuordnung
activities.description: Learners receive a worksheet with 8 illustrated cartoon figures, each showing a clear symptom (e.g., a person holding their head, a person with a red throat, a person with a thermometer). Task: Match each picture to the correct sentence from a given list (e.g., 'Er hat Kopfschmerzen.', 'Sie hat Fieber.'). Then learners write the matching sentence themselves in the space provided. Peer-check in pairs. Review together. Teacher highlights the use of er/sie (he/she) and links back to Week 2 pronouns.

activities.title: Beim Arzt – Rollenspiel
activities.description: Learners practice a structured role-play dialogue in pairs: Person A = Patient, Person B = Arzt/Ärztin (Doctor). A dialogue scaffold is provided on a card: Arzt: 'Guten Tag! Was fehlt Ihnen?' / Patient: 'Guten Tag! Ich habe ___schmerzen. / Ich habe Fieber.' / Arzt: 'Seit wann?' / Patient: 'Seit ___ Tag/en.' / Arzt: 'Ich gebe Ihnen ein Rezept. Gute Besserung!' / Patient: 'Danke schön. Auf Wiedersehen.' Introduce 'Seit wann?' and simple time expressions: seit einem Tag, seit zwei Tagen, seit einer Woche. Learners practice the dialogue 3 times, switching roles each time and changing the complaint. Teacher monitors, notes errors for delayed correction. 2–3 pairs perform in front of class at the end. Note for Vietnamese learners: the formal 'Ihnen' (dative of Sie) is introduced passively here as a fixed phrase; deep grammar analysis is deferred to A2.
materials: Dialogue scaffold card (laminated or printed, one per pair)

activities.title: Reflexion und Zusammenfassung
activities.description: Teacher conducts a rapid whole-class review: displays 5 images of sick people and cold-calls learners to produce sentences ('Was hat er/sie?'). Teacher then elicits from learners: 'Was haben Sie heute gelernt?' – learners respond in simple German sentences or via thumbs up/down for comprehension check. Teacher previews homework and next week's topic (Lebensmittel & Einkaufen). Provide a summary reference card.

lesson_plans.grammar_focus: Verb 'haben' in present tense (ich habe, du hast, er/sie/es hat) used to express physical complaints; German compound nouns with '-schmerzen' (Kopf+Schmerzen); Introduction to 'seit' + dative for duration of illness (passive recognition at A1); Gender and articles of body part nouns (der/die/das) with plural forms
lesson_plans.cultural_note: In German-speaking countries (Germany, Austria, Switzerland – DACH region), visiting a doctor (Arzt/Ärztin) requires an appointment (ein Termin) in most cases, unlike in Vietnam where walk-in visits are standard. The greeting 'Gute Besserung!' (Get well soon!) is used widely and is an important social expression. Pharmacies (Apotheken) are indicated by a red 'A' sign and pharmacists (Apotheker/in) play a key role in primary healthcare advice – they can recommend medication for minor complaints without a prescription. In Germany, statutory health insurance (Krankenversicherung) covers most of the population; learners planning to live/work in Germany should be aware that showing your Versichertenkarte (health insurance card) is required at every doctor visit. In Austria and Switzerland, similar systems exist. It is also culturally normal in German workplaces to call in sick (sich krankmelden) and provide a doctor's note (Krankenschein/Attest) from the third day of illness.

homework.description: Learners complete three homework tasks to reinforce body vocabulary, health expressions, and writing skills practiced in class.
exercises: Exercise 1 – Körperteil-Kreuzworträtsel: Complete a crossword puzzle using German body part clues in English or Vietnamese (10 body parts). Available as printed handout or digital link.

Exercise 2 – Schreib-Aufgabe: Write 5 sentences describing health complaints of 5 different people using different pronouns (ich, du, er, sie, wir). Example: 'Mein Vater hat Rückenschmerzen.' Use the dialogue scaffold from class as reference.

Exercise 3 – Hörübung (optional digital): Listen to a 2-minute audio recording of a doctor-patient dialogue (provided via class WhatsApp group or learning platform). Note down: What is the patient's complaint? How long has he/she been ill? Answer in Vietnamese is acceptable for this task.

Exercise 4 – Vocabulary flashcards: Create 10 paper flashcards (German word + article on front, drawing + Vietnamese translation on back) for body parts not yet fully memorized, using the bilingual vocabulary card as reference.

formative: Exit ticket at end of Session 1: Learners write German word + article for 5 pointed body parts – teacher reviews before Session 2 to identify gaps
Teacher observation during TPR activity: checks speed and accuracy of body part identification
Peer-check during symptom-matching worksheet: teacher circulates and notes recurring errors for whole-class feedback
Monitoring of role-play in Session 2: teacher uses a simple checklist (correct vocabulary use / correct article / comprehensible pronunciation / appropriate phrases) for each pair
Wrap-up cold-calling in Session 2: spot-check understanding of 'er hat / sie hat' sentence production
assessment.summative: End-of-week mini-quiz (administered at start of Week 8, 10 minutes): Part 1 – Label 8 body parts on a blank diagram with correct article (8 points). Part 2 – Match 5 symptoms to correct German phrases (5 points). Part 3 – Write 3 sentences about health complaints using 'Ich habe...' or 'Er/Sie hat...' (6 points). Total: 19 points. Pass mark: 13/19 (68%). Feedback returned within one class day.

differentiation.struggling_learners: Provide a fully labelled body diagram (with articles color-coded) that learners may keep on their desk throughout activities as a reference scaffold. Reduce the vocabulary target to 10 core body parts (head, eyes, nose, mouth, ears, hands, feet, stomach, back, throat) before extending to full list. Allow Vietnamese annotations on all worksheets. During role-play, provide a fully scripted dialogue rather than a scaffold, so learners focus on pronunciation and delivery rather than language production. Pair with a more confident learner during communicative activities. Offer additional practice using free app 'Quizlet' with a pre-made set of the week's vocabulary (teacher shares link). Break compound noun explanation into smaller steps: first 'Kopf' + 'Schmerzen' separately, then combined.
differentiation.advanced_learners: Extension task: Write a short paragraph (4–5 sentences) describing a sick friend or family member, including what they have, since when, and what the doctor recommended. Introduce additional vocabulary: die Erkältung (cold), die Grippe (flu), die Allergie (allergy), das Krankenhaus (hospital), die Tablette (tablet). Challenge learners to create their own original role-play scenario (e.g., at a pharmacy rather than at the doctor) without a scaffold. Introduce the modal verb 'müssen' passively: 'Sie müssen viel Wasser trinken.' as a fixed phrase for medical advice. Encourage learners to research DACH health system differences (Germany vs Austria vs Switzerland) and report back in 2–3 sentences.

review_from_previous: Week 1–2: Greetings and formal/informal address (Sie vs. du) – activated in doctor role-play context using formal 'Sie'
Week 3–4: Definite and indefinite articles (der/die/das) – revisited through body part gender assignment
Week 3–4: Verb 'haben' conjugation (ich habe, du hast, er hat) – core structure for expressing health complaints
Week 5: Numbers 1–100 – used in pain scale rating and 'seit X Tagen' expressions
Week 6: Verb 'sein' (ich bin, du bist, er ist) – used in 'Ich bin krank / müde / gesund'
spaced_repetition.preview_next_week: Week 8 will focus on 'Lebensmittel & Einkaufen' (Food & Shopping). The health context from Week 7 provides a natural bridge: learners will connect healthy eating habits to body wellbeing. Vocabulary such as 'Ich kaufe Obst – das ist gut für die Gesundheit' links both topics. The formal shopping dialogue (Verkäufer/Kunde) mirrors the formal register practiced in the doctor role-play, reinforcing polite formal German (Sie-form) across real-world contexts.

learning_objectives: Can name at least 10 common hobbies and leisure activities in German and use them in simple sentences
Can ask and answer the question 'Was machst du in deiner Freizeit?' using 'ich + verb' constructions
Can express frequency of activities using basic adverbs: immer, oft, manchmal, selten, nie
prerequisite_knowledge: Present tense conjugation of regular verbs (machen, spielen, hören, lesen) for ich/du/er/sie
Basic sentence structure: Subject + Verb + Object (SVO)
Numbers 1–7 for days of the week (covered in Week 5)
Modal verb 'mögen' in simple form: ich mag / ich mag nicht
Definite and indefinite articles (der/die/das, ein/eine) from Weeks 2–4
Basic question formation with W-Fragen: Was, Wer, Wo, Wann

sessions.title: Hobbys entdecken – Discovering Hobbies

activities.title: Bilderrätsel: Was ist das Hobby?
activities.description: Teacher displays 8–10 flashcard images of common hobbies (Fußball spielen, Musik hören, lesen, kochen, reisen, schwimmen, tanzen, fotografieren) on the board or screen. Learners in pairs point to each image and attempt to guess the German word. Teacher confirms answers and drills pronunciation chorally. Special attention given to Vietnamese learners on German vowel sounds ü, ö and the 'ch' in 'kochen' — teacher demonstrates mouth position and contrasts with Vietnamese phoneme approximations. Duration: 10 minutes.
materials: Flashcard image set (printed A5 or projected)
Vietnamese–German mini glossary handout for reference

activities.title: Vokabelliste: Meine Hobbys
activities.description: Teacher introduces the 20 target vocabulary words using a structured handout. Each word is presented with: German noun/verb phrase, article where applicable, IPA phonetic transcription, a sample sentence, and a Vietnamese translation gloss. Teacher models each word with exaggerated pronunciation, learners repeat in chorus (3x), then in rows, then individually. Teacher highlights collocations: 'Fußball SPIELEN' vs 'Gitarre SPIELEN' vs 'Tennis SPIELEN' — all use 'spielen'. Learners underline the verbs in each phrase to notice patterns. This addresses Vietnamese learners' tendency to omit verbs in speech.
materials: Structured vocabulary handout (20 items with Vietnamese glosses)
Audio recording of native speaker pronunciation (optional MP3 file)

activities.title: Satzbauspiel: Ich spiele, ich höre, ich lese…
activities.description: Learners receive a sentence-building worksheet with three columns: (A) Subject pronouns ich/du/er/sie, (B) verb bank (spielen, hören, lesen, kochen, machen, gehen, schwimmen), (C) hobby nouns/objects (Fußball, Musik, Bücher, Yoga, Fotos, ins Kino). Learners construct 6 grammatically correct sentences by matching columns. Teacher circulates and monitors. Key grammar point reinforced: verb must be in second position. After individual work, pairs compare sentences and correct each other. Teacher reviews on the board with whole class, eliciting answers.

activities.title: Mini-Interview: Was machst du in deiner Freizeit?
activities.description: Learners practice a short 4-line dialogue using a model on the board: A: 'Was machst du in deiner Freizeit?' B: 'Ich [verb] [hobby]. Und du?' A: 'Ich [verb] [hobby].' B: 'Interessant!' or 'Das mag ich auch!' Pairs rehearse the dialogue 2x, then swap roles. Teacher monitors for correct verb conjugation. After practice, 3–4 volunteer pairs perform in front of the class. Teacher gives positive feedback and gentle correction. Vietnamese learner note: coach learners to use rising intonation on questions, as Vietnamese tonal system may cause flat intonation in German questions.

sessions.title: Wie oft? – Talking About Frequency and Preferences

activities.title: Schnelle Wiederholung: Hobby-Vokabular
activities.description: Teacher shows 6 hobby images rapidly (2 seconds each) on the projector. Learners call out the German word/phrase. Then teacher does a quick 'Thumbs Up / Thumbs Down' comprehension check: teacher reads a sentence (e.g., 'Ich spiele Gitarre') and learners show thumbs up if correct German or thumbs down if something is wrong (teacher occasionally inserts errors like 'Ich spiele Musik' for Musik hören). This activates prior learning and addresses any vocabulary gaps from Session 1.
materials: Projected hobby images (same set from Session 1)

activities.title: Frequenzadverbien: immer, oft, manchmal, selten, nie
activities.description: Teacher draws a frequency scale on the board (0%–100%) and places the five adverbs: nie (0%) – selten (25%) – manchmal (50%) – oft (75%) – immer (100%). Vietnamese translation equivalents are written below each adverb. Teacher models sentences: 'Ich spiele immer Fußball.' / 'Ich gehe manchmal ins Kino.' / 'Ich lese nie Bücher.' Teacher emphasizes that the adverb typically comes directly after the conjugated verb in statements. Learners copy the scale into their notebooks. Teacher then does a sentence transformation drill: teacher says 'Ich spiele Fußball' and holds up a frequency card; learners must call out the complete new sentence. Repeat 8–10 times with different verbs and adverbs.
materials: Frequency adverb flashcards (5 cards: immer, oft, manchmal, selten, nie)

activities.title: Umfrage: Wie oft machst du das?
activities.description: Each learner receives a survey grid with 6 hobbies listed in rows (Fußball spielen, kochen, lesen, tanzen, Musik hören, ins Kino gehen) and 5 frequency columns. Learners first complete the grid for themselves (5 minutes). Then they stand up and conduct a 'Mingle' activity: they ask 2 different classmates 'Wie oft [verb + hobby]?' and record responses. Sentence stems are on the board for support: 'Wie oft spielst du Fußball?' / 'Wie oft hörst du Musik?'. After mingling, pairs share one interesting finding with the class: '[Name] spielt oft Fußball, aber ich spiele selten.' This activity recycles du-form conjugation from previous weeks.
materials: Sentence stem support card on board
activities.interaction_pattern: individual, then mingle, then pairs reporting to whole class

activities.title: Mein Freizeitprofil – My Leisure Profile (Short Writing)
activities.description: Learners write 5–6 sentences about their own free-time activities using the model text on the board: 'In meiner Freizeit [verb] ich [hobby]. Ich [verb] [frequency] [hobby]. Ich mag [hobby], aber ich mag [hobby] nicht.' Teacher provides a scaffolded writing frame on the handout with blanks to fill in. Learners choose their own genuine hobbies to make it personally meaningful. After writing, learners read their profile to their partner who listens and asks one follow-up question using 'Wie oft?' Teacher collects written profiles for formative assessment review. Vietnamese learner note: anticipate confusion between 'spielen' and 'machen' — display a clear colocation reference on the board throughout the task.
materials: Vocabulary handout from Session 1 as reference

vocabulary_target: die Freizeit – free time / leisure time
Musik hören – to listen to music
ins Kino gehen – to go to the cinema
Sport machen / Sport treiben – to do sport
gern – gladly / with pleasure (used to express liking: ich spiele gern)
lesson_plans.grammar_focus: Present tense verb conjugation (ich/du/er/sie) with hobby collocations (spielen, hören, machen, gehen + infinitive). Placement of frequency adverbs (immer, oft, manchmal, selten, nie) in the middle field (Mittelfeld) of German sentences — directly after the conjugated verb in main clauses. Introduction of 'gern' + verb as a way to express preference (ich spiele gern Fußball = I like playing football), contrasting with 'mögen' + noun (ich mag Fußball) introduced in earlier weeks.
lesson_plans.cultural_note: In German-speaking countries (Deutschland, Österreich, Schweiz – DACH region), leisure time (Freizeit) is considered culturally important and is clearly separated from work life. Germans famously value 'Feierabend' — the moment work ends and personal time begins — and this boundary is respected socially. Popular hobbies in Germany include Wandern (hiking), Radfahren (cycling), Vereinssport (club sports), and Lesen. Germany has one of the highest rates of club membership in the world — many people pursue hobbies through organized 'Vereine' (clubs/associations), from football clubs to choral societies to hiking groups. In Vietnam, leisure activities are often more communal and family-oriented; this contrast can be a rich discussion point. The concept of 'Hobbys haben' is also something Germans commonly discuss in job interviews and social introductions, making this vocabulary highly practical.

homework.description: Learners complete three tasks to consolidate vocabulary and grammar from the week's sessions and prepare for the next lesson on daily routines.
